caption: Figure 13.0.1: LLMs can manufacture training examples on demand. The trick is making sure the synthetic output is as nourishing as the real thing.
Figure 13.1.2: Every great synthetic dataset starts with a handful of seed examples. Plant them well, and watch your training data bloom.
Figure 13.2.1: The LLM generation pipeline: prompts go in one end, polished training examples come out the other. Quality control not included by default.
Figure 13.2.2: Prompt templates are the cookie cutters of synthetic data generation. Same shape, different fillings, consistently delicious results.
Figure 13.2.3: Evol-Instruct in action: simple instructions evolve into increasingly complex ones, like Darwinian selection for prompt difficulty.
Figure 13.4.1: LLM-assisted labeling is like having a sorting hat for your data. It is not always right, but it is fast and surprisingly good at the job.
Figure 13.4.2: Active learning: why label everything when you can strategically fish for the samples that teach your model the most?
Figure 13.4.3: Noisy labels are like an orchestra where a few musicians are playing the wrong piece. The challenge is figuring out who is off-key.
Figure 13.5.1: Weak supervision lets multiple imperfect labeling functions vote on the answer. Democracy for data labels, where the majority usually wins.
Figure 13.6.1: Reasoning chains are like dominos: each step triggers the next, and if one falls wrong, the whole conclusion topples.
Figure 13.6.2: Rejection sampling for reasoning data is just gold panning with extra steps. Generate many traces, keep only the nuggets that actually reach the correct answer.
Figure 13.6.3: Red-teaming with synthetic data: one LLM throws punches while the other learns to dodge. The best defense is a good sparring partner.
Figure 13.7.1: The augmentation kaleidoscope: one example goes in, and a spectrum of label-preserving variations fans out the other side.
Figure 14.0.1: Fine-tuning is teaching an old (very large) dog new tricks, one carefully chosen gradient step at a time.
Figure 14.1.2: The eternal question: should you fine-tune or just prompt better? This decision tree saves you from weeks of unnecessary GPU bills.
Figure 14.1.3: As task-specific performance improves, general capabilities may degrade. The optimal checkpoint balances both.
Figure 14.2.1: Sequence packing is Tetris for training data. Fit as many examples as possible into each batch, and watch your GPU utilization score soar.
Figure 14.3.1: Catastrophic forgetting: your model aced the new task but forgot everything else. It is like cramming for one exam and blanking on all the others.
Figure 14.7.1: Without context extension, perplexity degrades sharply beyond the training window. Context extension techniques maintain quality at longer lengths.
Figure 15.0.1: Why retrain billions of parameters when a few clever sticky notes on the right layers can do the job? PEFT adapters are the ultimate lightweight upgrade.
Figure 15.1.1: LoRA in a nutshell: instead of rewriting the whole textbook, just slap a sticky note on the relevant pages. Same knowledge, fraction of the effort.
Figure 15.1.2: QLoRA: take your already-compact quantized model and add custom decals. You get personalization without needing a bigger garage.
Figure 15.2.1: PEFT methods are like accessories for your base model. Mix and match adapters until you find the look that works for your task.
